text: F. Fighter.
It's the most famous letter in military aviation, and today it covers multirole jets that also strike targets on the ground.
The F thirty-five should have been the F twenty-four, the next number in line. Instead, it kept the number of its demonstrator, the X thirty-five.
And the F one seventeen Nighthawk got an F, even though it was built for ground attack.
A. Attack.
An attack aircraft is built to hit targets on land or at sea.
Today, the A ten is the only aircraft in the Air Force that still carries a plain A.
B. Bomber.
Bombers fly long-range strike missions.
The newest one is the B twenty-one. Its number was chosen because it's the first bomber of the twenty-first century. By the rules, it would have been the B three.
C. Cargo.
C means transport, like the C one thirty Hercules.

And the C one thirty shows how the whole system works. Add one more letter in front, and the same airframe becomes a gunship, a rescue plane, a special operations plane, an electronic warfare plane, or a tanker.
K. Tanker.
Put a K in front of a C, and you get a tanker, like the K C forty-six.
K exists as a basic mission too, but no ordinary aircraft has ever been given it the way the rules intended.
Some names simply copy the maker. A tanker sold to other countries became the K C seven sixty-seven, straight from Boeing's model number.
E. Electronic.
As a modified mission, E means electronic warfare, like the E C one thirty.
As a basic mission, it means special electronics, for aircraft built around radars and sensors.
H. Rescue, and helicopter.
H can show up twice in the same name.
In the H H sixty G, the first H means search and rescue, and the second H means helicopter. Many of them started life as Black Hawks that were modified for rescue.
M. Multi-mission.
M aircraft fly combat and special operations, like the M C one thirty.
And the M Q nine Reaper reads as multi-mission, unmanned, design number nine.
U. Utility.
U aircraft fly support missions, like the U H sixty Black Hawk.
Utility was once used as a cover. The U two spy plane was labeled utility to hide what it really did.
R. Reconnaissance.
R is for spy missions.
The S R seventy-one Blackbird was set to be called the R S seventy-one, but Air Force chief Curtis LeMay preferred S R, for strategic reconnaissance. And S R is what stuck.
W. Weather.
W means weather reconnaissance.
That's why the Air Force's hurricane hunters are W C one thirties.
V. VIP, and vertical takeoff.
In front, V means VIP transport. The President's 747 is the V C twenty-five, and his newest helicopter is the V H ninety-two.
Before the dash, V means vertical or short takeoff, like the M V twenty-two Osprey.
L. Cold weather.
L means modified for cold weather. The L C one thirty has skis, for landing on ice.
Q. Unmanned.
Q means drone.
There's even a letter for the ground stations that fly them: D, for the U A V control segment.
P. Patrol.
P means maritime patrol, for aircraft that watch the sea.
Today's main one is the P eight Poseidon, a Navy jet built on a Boeing 737.
S. Anti-submarine.
S is for hunting submarines. Before the dash, S means something completely different: a spaceplane.
The S three Viking flew from aircraft carriers to hunt submarines.
T. Trainer.
The T six Texan Two skipped the numbers four and five, as a tribute to the original T six trainer.
O. Observation.
O means observation, like spotting targets for other aircraft. The new O A one K Skyraider Two borrowed the name of the old A one Skyraider.
X. Experimental.
In front of everything, X means experimental. That's where the F thirty-five started, as the X thirty-five.
Experimental aircraft flown by manufacturers or by NASA often get X numbers too.
Y. Prototype.
The jet that won the competition was the Y F twenty-two. The one that entered service was the F twenty-two.
G. Grounded.
As a prefix, G means permanently grounded. Before the dash, G means glider.
J and N. Special test.
J means a temporary special test, and the aircraft goes back to normal service. N means it never does.

The whole system dates to nineteen sixty-two. Before that, the Navy and the Air Force named their aircraft differently, and the same fighter was the F four H Phantom to one and the F one ten to the other.
After the change, it became simply the F four.
And after the letters come the numbers. In nineteen sixty-two, the counts were restarted, which is why they suddenly got small again.
The last letter marks the version: A, then B, then C. I and O are skipped, so they're never confused with one and zero.
And the number thirteen has been skipped in many series, for superstition.
Which aircraft name should I decode next? Tell me in the comments.
